t: or a person who swears to utter. And later in the verse it says: 'to do evil or to do good,' meaning both for the negative and the positive. The Sages learned that the oath applies both to the past and to the future (Mishnah Shevuot 3:5).
in things that he is able to do. For one who swears about things he is unable to do, this is a vain oath, as below halakhah 7.

and how for the future etc.. For an oath about the future, the example 'So-and-so will speak with so-and-so' is not mentioned here, because it does not depend on the one who swears but on someone else (see below 5:1-2).
and you shall not swear by My name falsely. Both to lie in fact regarding what already happened in an oath about the past, and to cause the oath to be false in the future in an oath about the future.

if deliberately, he receives lashes. Although when one swears that he will do something and did not do it he does not receive lashes, since it is a prohibition without an act (as below 4:20-21), sometimes he receives lashes even in this case, for example if he swore to eat the loaf and threw it into the sea, for he transgressed his oath by performing an act (Penei Yehoshua, Shevuot 4:1, and see Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh).

unintentionally. For example, he swore that he did not eat and he did eat, and when he swore he knew that he had eaten and even knew that it is forbidden to swear falsely in this way, but did not know that one is liable for a sacrifice for such an oath (for the definition of unintentional see below 3:6-7).
a sliding-scale offering. A sin offering whose type varies according to the person's financial situation (Hilchot Shegagot 1:4).
for there is no doubt to any person in the world that it is so. See below 5:22.
to a person of sound. Mind.
who swore to nullify the commandment. And if he transgressed and swore, he must fulfill the commandment, and receives lashes for a vain oath (below 5:14).

that he will not wrap himself in tzitzit. That he will wear a four-cornered garment and not attach tzitzit to it. But one who swears not to wear a garment with tzitzit does not nullify the commandment, because he is not obligated to wear it (see Hilchot Tzitzit 3:11, Radbaz; and see R. Yosef Kafih, that the Rambam's words here follow what he initially held, that a person is obligated to wrap himself in tzitzit).

and if he was deliberate, he receives lashes. Although ordinarily one does not receive lashes for a prohibition without an act, a vain oath is an exception to this rule, because it says of it, 'for the Lord will not hold guiltless one who takes His name in vain' (Exodus 20:7, Deuteronomy 5:11), and the Sages learned that the court clears him by means of lashes (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2; and see Babylonian Talmud, Shevuot 21a).
defrauded him. For example, he did not pay him wages for his work.
and one does not give lashes for this prohibition. Because it has no act.

and this oath is called the oath of deposit. Although it also includes an oath about a loan or a robbery and the like, it is called the oath of deposit because denial of a deposit is more common and the verse begins with it (Radbaz).
pays. To the depositor or the lender and the like.

with the addition of a fifth. He adds to the principal a quarter of its value, so that together with the principal the addition is a fifth (see Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 4:5). He pays the fifth only if he confessed on his own; but if witnesses testified against him and he stands by his denial, he pays only the principal (Hilchot Gezelah 7:8).
a definite guilt offering. A guilt offering that comes for a definite sin, different from a provisional guilt offering that comes for a doubtful sin (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:6).
for a deposit. That he placed in his hand money in partnership or as a loan.

and it does not say 'and it is hidden' regarding it. Because in this case the word 'and it is hidden' is not stated, which means that it was unintentional, this implies there is no distinction between unintentional and intentional (unlike the oath of utterance, above halakhah 3).
and exempt from everything. Both from paying the fifth and from the sacrifice, and he does not transgress the prohibition 'you shall not deal falsely' (see also below 3:6).
and exempt. From the fifth and from the sacrifice, but he transgressed the prohibition 'you shall not deal falsely,' for he knew that the money was with him (Radbaz).
these are compelled and exempt even from the sacrifice. See also below 3:6.
and he answered amen. But if he was silent and said nothing, he is not like one who swore (Kesef Mishneh).
hin. Yes.
whether to make him liable for lashes. For example, he was deliberate in an oath of utterance or a vain oath.
or to make him liable for a sacrifice. When he was unintentional in an oath of utterance, and when he was unintentional or deliberate in an oath of deposit and an oath of testimony.

by the Unique Name. The names of God that may not be erased (for their enumeration see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:2; for the meaning of the expression see also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 2:7, Hilchot Keriat Shema 3:5).
or by one of the epithets. By which the Holy One, blessed be He, is praised (Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:5).
and the like in any language. For the names by which gentiles call the Holy One, blessed be He, are like all the epithets (Hilchot Sanhedrin 26:3).
by a curse... one who eats such-and-such and ate it, this is swearing falsely. The swearer's intent is to place a curse on himself if he eats, but he spoke in euphemistic language.
this is swearing falsely. And he is liable for an oath of utterance.
that I will not eat, and he ate. An oath of utterance.
that this is a woman and he is a man. A vain oath.
that I have nothing of yours in my possession, and he does. An oath of deposit.
that I know no testimony for you, and he does. An oath of testimony.
he is liable. For this is a complete oath, and he is liable for every oath according to its laws.
as we have explained. Above halakhah 2.
stammerers. Whose tongues are mixed up and confused.
miha. So it is in several manuscripts. In the printed editions the reading is 'moha,' and so it is in Mishnah Nedarim 1:2 in the Rambam's manuscript (and in other versions of the Mishnah: 'mota').
no, no, twice. For example, he said, 'I will not eat, I will not eat.'

this is like one who swore. This expression is considered an oath, for we find that the Holy One, blessed be He, said, 'and never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood' (Genesis 9:11), and the prophet says, 'as I swore that the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth' (Isaiah 54:9), from which it follows that saying 'no' twice is the language of an oath.
and likewise 'right hand' is an oath and 'left hand' is an oath, as it says, 'The Lord swore by His right hand and by His mighty arm'. From which it follows that this is the language of an oath.
and likewise one who says 'by utterance' that I will not do such and such. As in the language of the verse: 'or a person who swears, speaking rashly with his lips...' (Leviticus 5:4).

since he expressed it in the language of an oath. Although 'issar' (prohibition) is the language of a vow (Hilchot Nedarim 1:1), since he expressed it in the language of an oath, which refers to the person's action (unlike a vow, which refers to the object forbidden to the person - see ibid. 3:7), we treat it as an oath and not as a vow.
he is exempt. From a sacrifice or lashes, but he is obligated to fulfill his friend's oath, as below.

and this one cannot extend by an oath, so he is exempt. One who extends in vows is one who applies a vow made about a certain object to an additional object, which is possible because a vow applies to the object and therefore another object can be extended onto it (Hilchot Nedarim 3:3-4); but an oath applies to the person and the person is not forbidden, so one cannot extend onto it.
and he resolved in his heart. He decided.
and they warned him. They warned him before he ate that he may not eat because of his oath and that he will be punished if he eats.

they do not listen to him. Because after the warning he admitted he intended to eat, or he did not claim at the time of the warning that his intention was otherwise, he cannot claim it now, and he receives lashes.
and once he saw that they testified against him. After he saw that they testified against him.
he is forbidden wheat bread. Only, though he did not say so explicitly.
when the judges administer an oath to the one who swears. In cases where he must swear in court (as below 11:18).
and it is the time it takes a student to say to the teacher 'Peace upon you, Rabbi'. The time it takes to say these three words.
I regretted. I regretted.
I retracted. I changed my mind.
for this resembles one who errs. One who uttered with his lips what was not in his heart, as above halakhah 11.
until he utters the retraction with his mouth as he did the oath. Just as in an oath his mouth and heart must be the same, so also in regret.
from these four kinds of oaths. Mentioned above 1:1.
and likewise one who swears from the outset under duress, as we have explained. Above 1:10.
a coercer. A violent person who can harm another's property or person (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nedarim 3:3).
therefore. Since one who swears under duress is exempt, in certain cases one swears even at the outset.
to the charamin. Highway robbers and bandits (ibid.), who do not kill.
and to the haragin. Robbers who kill over monetary matters.
and to tax collectors. Those who collect customs.
concerning which tax collector did they say. That one swears to him at the outset and is exempt from the oath.

a tax collector who stands on his own etc.. Such a tax collector is a robber. But if he takes tax according to the king's decree, one does not swear to him, because it is the king's law and there is no robbery here.
as will be explained in Hilchot Gezelah. 5:11.
on a condition that exempts. On a condition that will exempt him from fulfilling the oath, as below.

and although these things in the heart are not things. In other laws, no force is given to the thought of the heart (see, for example, Hilchot Mechirah 11:9), and here we rely on it because of the duress.

for example, he swore to the coercer that he will not eat meat, without specification. That he forbids himself to eat meat if he has money improperly, or if he did not pay the tax properly, and the like.
exaggeration. Hyperbole.
without less or more. Exactly.

for example, he erred regarding a deposit and testimony. For example, he forgot that he has his friend's money, or forgot that he knows testimony for his friend, or mistakenly thought there is no prohibition in these oaths.
as we have explained. Above 1:10, 1:13.
and if it is a false oath. An oath of utterance.
for which they are liable for a sliding-scale sacrifice. As explained above 1:3.

for the oath was forgotten by him, how it was, yet he remembers the object on which he swore. The Sages learned that such a lapse of the oath is considered unintentional and not duress, and they are liable for it (see Kesef Mishneh).
because of the suffering. Because of hunger.

for he does not return from his knowledge. When he learned that suffering does not permit eating, no new knowledge arose in him concerning the prohibition of the oath, for he knew that one is liable for a sacrifice for forbidden eating, but thought that his suffering permitted him to eat. And he is not liable for a sacrifice, for the sacrifice liability for unintentional transgression applies when at the time he transgressed the oath he lacked knowledge concerning the very prohibition of the oath (for example, he did not know that one is liable for a sacrifice for the oath), and afterward he learned of it (see Lechem Mishneh).
for eating less than an olive-bulk is not eating. And therefore we interpret his intent as an olive-bulk or more (compare Hilchot Nedarim 1:5).

and he is like one who eats half a measure of carrion, treifot and the like. Although it is forbidden by the Torah to eat even a small amount of them, he receives lashes only if he ate an olive-bulk of them (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 14:2). Here too the prohibition of eating applies even to less than an olive-bulk, even any amount, but he does not receive lashes (Radbaz and Kesef Mishneh).
and if he said, 'I swear that I will not eat this thing,' and ate it, he is liable. Because he swore regarding eating a specific thing, and ate it.
one mustard seed. Which is a small thing, even less than half an olive-bulk.
he swore that he would not taste anything, and ate any amount, he is liable. For tasting means even the smallest amount.
therefore. Because drinking is included in eating, if he drinks and eats it is as if he ate two eatings under one lapse of the oath (as below halakhah 5; Radbaz).
like other prohibitions. Like other prohibitions on drinking, for example the nazirite's drinking of wine (Hilchot Nezirut 5:2) or drinking gentile wine (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 11:3).
he is liable only once. And he does not receive lashes for each kind separately.
and all of them combine to an olive-bulk. If he ate an olive-bulk in total from all of them, they combine to make him liable for lashes or a sacrifice, because they were included in one oath.
for drinking is included in eating. As above halakhah 3.
for he said 'bread and bread and bread' only to distinguish and make him liable for each one. But if he said, 'I swear not to eat bread of wheat and barley and spelt,' he is liable only once.
pressing. Urging.

and when he went back and specified, he revealed his mind that he obligated himself in an oath for each kind separately. But if his friend said nothing to him and he said on his own, 'I swear that I will not drink wine and milk and honey,' he is not liable until he eats from all of them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 3:4).
therefore. Because he is liable for each one separately.
they do not combine with one another. To the eating measure that makes him liable.
since they are separate for sin offerings. For he is liable for a separate sacrifice for each.

they are like fat and blood, which do not combine to an olive-bulk. If he ate a little fat and a little blood, he does not receive lashes, because each prohibition stands on its own and they do not combine with one another.
as we have explained in Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot. 4:16.

I swear that I will not eat this loaf, or that I will not eat it. Since he used the language of eating by itself, his intent is not to eat even an olive-bulk; and what he added, 'this loaf' or 'it,' is meant to distinguish it from other bread, but he does not intend to forbid himself only the eating of the whole loaf (Kesef Mishneh).

I swear that I will not eat it - he is not liable until he eats all of it. Since he did not use the language of eating by itself but attached the prohibition of eating to the loaf, he means the whole loaf.

he is liable only once. For the second oath does not take effect, because in the first oath he already swore regarding an olive-bulk, and certainly not to eat the whole, and in such a case an oath does not take effect on an oath, as below.

for an oath does not take effect on an oath. Just as a prohibition does not take effect on a prohibition (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:8, and see below halakhah 11), so the second oath does not take effect on the first, for in the first oath he had already sworn not to eat anything today (but if he ate it the next day he is liable because of his oath not to eat it, for the first oath is no longer in force and so the second oath takes effect - Kesef Mishneh and Radbaz).
and he became liable by two oaths. If deliberate, he receives two sets of lashes, and if unintentional he brings two sacrifices.

as we have explained in Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot. 14:18-19; that although a prohibition does not take effect on a prohibition, when the second prohibition includes, besides the first prohibition, other things that were permitted, the second prohibition takes effect too.

he is liable only once. For the second and third oaths do not take effect on the first, because if he is forbidden to eat eight, all the more so is he forbidden to eat nine and ten, and an oath does not take effect on an oath.

and he again swore that he would not eat figs and grapes together. That he not eat figs and grapes at once, and since the oath took effect on the grapes, it also took effect on the figs (as above halakhah 11).

he is not liable for the grapes because they are like half a measure. Since he set aside a sacrifice for eating the figs, it does not combine with the grapes he ate now, and although he is forbidden to eat them, he is not liable for a sacrifice.
that he would not eat ten. Certain loaves.

and again swore that he would not eat ten and nine. These ten on which he swore previously, plus nine other specific loaves; and since an oath took effect on the nine, it also took effect on the ten, although he had already sworn on them in his earlier oath (Lechem Mishneh).
I swear that I will not eat this large loaf if I ate this small loaf. So the large loaf is the forbidden loaf and the small loaf is the condition loaf.
and afterward ate the large one deliberately, he is liable. For the liability stems from his state of awareness at the time he ate the forbidden loaf and not at the time he ate the condition loaf.
and forgot and ate the large one, and it seemed to him that it had not yet been forbidden. For example, he forgot that he had eaten the condition loaf.
exempt. For at the time of eating the forbidden loaf he was unintentional.
ate both unintentionally, exempt. For in this case too he ate the forbidden loaf unintentionally.
whether he ate the large one first. And if he afterward eats the small one, which is the condition loaf, it turns out that he retroactively violated his oath.
or last. And he already ate the small one, which is the condition loaf, and is forbidden the large one.

liable. Since he was deliberate in eating the forbidden loaf. But if he ate the large loaf, which is the forbidden loaf, at first deliberately, and afterward ate the small loaf, which is the condition loaf, unintentionally, he is not liable for lashes since he was unintentional in eating the small one, and not liable for a sacrifice since he was deliberate in eating the large one (Lechem Mishneh).

and forgot the condition and ate one of them and ate the second deliberately, he is liable. For the first became the condition loaf and the second the forbidden loaf, and he ate the forbidden loaf deliberately.
if unintentional, he brings a sliding-scale sacrifice. As above 1:3.
if deliberate, he does not receive lashes, for he did not perform an act. And one does not give lashes for a prohibition without an act (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
that he did not eat, and he did eat, though he performed no act. And what he ate is not considered an act because he ate in full permission, but afterward he swore that he had not eaten (Radbaz).
that I will not eat of yours. That I will not eat from what is yours.
that I am not. That I am not.
pressing. Urging.

I swear that I will eat of yours. And because he had urged him previously, it implies that he means to say, 'I swear that I will not eat of yours' (Kesef Mishneh; and the Radbaz explained that the reason they interpret it so is that he had refused at first).

not an oath, I will not eat of yours. What I do not eat of yours will not be forbidden to me by oath, from which it follows that his intent is that what he does eat of his own will be forbidden to him by oath.
he is liable only once. For an oath does not take effect on an oath.

he is liable for an oath of utterance although it is not for the future. Although one is not liable for such an oath if he swears about the future, for it does not depend on him, in any case if he swore about the past he is liable.
disciplinary lashes. Lashes by rabbinic authority.

for he has no ability to fulfill this oath. And even if in the end his oath was fulfilled, they give him disciplinary lashes as a penalty, for he swore about something he cannot do (Me'irat Einayim, Choshen Mishpat).
and it turns out he causes a vain oath. For if others do not do what he said, his oath will be a vain oath.
and it turns out that when they warn him at the time he swears, it is a warning of doubt. For if the others fulfill his oath, he will not receive lashes.

for one gives lashes for it only if its prohibition is explicit, as will be explained in Hilchot Sanhedrin. 16:4. The commentators found the Rambam's words difficult, since there it is explained that one who transgresses a 'prohibition that is linked to a positive commandment' and was warned, although this is a warning of doubt (for if he transgresses the prohibition and fulfills the positive commandment he will not receive lashes), it is considered a warning. Some wrote to distinguish between the cases: there, at the time of the act, the person clearly transgressed the prohibition ('its prohibition is explicit'), and the doubt arises because afterward the person can fulfill the positive commandment and be exempt from lashes; here, by contrast, even at the time of the act there is no certainty that this is a vain oath (Mirkevet HaMishneh, and similarly see Yad Peshuta there).
are bound. Are obligated.
as we have explained. Above 2:1.
they accustomed. They caused.
exempt. For one can say that when he swore not to eat, he meant fit foods.

exempt from an oath of utterance. For these foods are not fit for eating because of their prohibition, and therefore in eating them he did not violate his oath but is liable for lashes for eating the forbidden food.
since they are important to him, eating them is called eating. And thereby he revealed his intent that when he swore he meant any kind of eating.

but for the future, where he swore that he would not eat and was called and was called, and ate them, it is not eating. Since one can say that this eating was by chance and is not considered eating, he cannot be held liable for violating the oath (and in the previous halakhah, where he swore that he would eat, and ate these things, he cannot be held liable because one can say that his eating was deliberate and is considered eating - Arukh HaShulchan 238:12).
as we have explained. Above halakhah 5.

for he is not sworn at Sinai regarding half a measure. And therefore he is not considered as swearing about the commandment, so that his oath would not take effect (see below halakhah 11). And although half a measure is forbidden by the Torah (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 14:2), its prohibition is not explicit in the Torah and therefore it is not among the things on which one is sworn from Mount Sinai (Radbaz).
he is liable for the oath. Because one is not sworn at Sinai regarding half a measure, the oath takes effect on him.
if he ate an olive-bulk, he is liable. Although these things are not fit for eating, since he swore about them explicitly, he is liable if he ate them.
perhaps he is liable for any amount etc.. And on the other hand, perhaps he is liable only for an olive-bulk, which is the eating measure, since he swore in the language of eating.
grape seed. Grape pits.

this is a doubt. Perhaps since it is usually eaten together with the grapes, his intent is eating an olive-bulk and he did not violate his oath; or perhaps since it is not eaten by itself, his intent is even any amount, and he violated his oath.

for he is forbidden grape seed in an olive-bulk. For a nazirite is forbidden everything that comes from the vine, including skins and seeds, and the measure of the prohibition is an olive-bulk (Hilchot Nezirut 5:2).

for his intent in his oath is only for the olive-bulk on which he is sworn. For he intended to swear in order to prod himself not to violate his nazirite prohibition (as below 11:3), and therefore there is no doubt that he did not intend less than an olive-bulk.
and an oath does not take effect on him. Since he is already sworn at Sinai not to eat it.

if he specified and said, 'I swear that I will not eat one grape seed,' and ate it, he is liable. Even if he is a nazirite, since he specified and said one, and he is not sworn at Sinai regarding one grape seed but regarding an olive-bulk, his oath takes effect, like one who swears about half a measure (above halakhah 7).
he is liable also for an oath of utterance. In addition to the liability under the prohibition of eating carrion and treifot.
as we have explained. Above 4:11.
not an oath of utterance. For he is sworn about it from Sinai (above halakhah 7).
and not a vain oath. Although he is obligated in this even without his oath, there is no vain oath here (and see below 11:3).
he receives lashes for a vain oath. For he swore to nullify the commandment (above 1:6).
whether he ate or did not eat. For he receives lashes for the oath itself.
and if he did not eat it, he is liable also for an oath of utterance. For in his first oath he swore that he would eat, and violated his oath.
exempt from an oath of utterance. For this oath does not take effect, since he is already sworn at Sinai to fulfill the commandments (above halakhah 7).
and he receives lashes for a vain oath. As above 1:6.
because he is commanded to testify. By Torah law (Hilchot Edut 1:1).
and it seems to me that he receives lashes for a vain oath. Like one who swears to nullify the commandment.
although he is not permitted. For a person is forbidden to injure himself (Hilchot Chovel 5:1).

although he is not permitted, an oath takes effect on him. Because this prohibition is not explicit in the Torah but is learned from the Sages' exposition, an oath takes effect on it (Radbaz, and as above halakhah 7).

swore to benefit others... an oath takes effect on him. Although he cannot swear to harm others, and so the verse 'to do evil or to do good' is not fully realized, the Sages learned that an oath takes effect in this case (Babylonian Talmud, Shevuot 27a).
and since the oath took effect on the other days, it took effect on the nights of Passover. See also above 4:11.

that he will not put on a garment for a year or two. That he will not wear a four-cornered garment with tzitzit, but without tzitzit (Radbaz, and see above 1:6 in the commentary). And because he said a year or two, the nights are included in his oath, and since the obligation of tzitzit does not apply at night, the oath takes effect on the night, and therefore it also takes effect on the day.
for it is a vain oath. For a person cannot survive without sleep for three days or without eating for seven days (above 1:7).
stay awake. Remain awake.
this is nothing. His intention does not help to exempt him from a vain oath.
that the sun is a hundred and seventy times larger than the earth. These things are based on an ancient estimate of the ratio of the earth and the sun (and see also Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 3:8).
he does not receive lashes for a vain oath. Although one who swears about a known thing, it is a vain oath (above 1:5), here, where it is not known, it is not a vain oath.
calculation of seasons and constellations. Calculating the time of the season and calculating the position of the constellations, which are part of the science of astronomy.
and gematriot. The science of measurement called geometry.
and regretted. And repented.
and his mind turned to another view. He changed his mind.
that arose. That newly developed.
asks. He goes to request annulment, and the sage asks him questions in order to release him.
this one asks... and they release him from his oath. However, one must be careful about this, and they undertake to release only for a mitzvah matter or because of great need (below 12:12).
from the tradition. The Sages' tradition.
with contempt. With disdain.
with his teacher's knowledge. With his permission.
provided that the three are gathered. That they were already together in one place.

but he may not gather them to release her at the outset. Some explain that the reason is that if he must go to the trouble of gathering them, it is preferable that his wife go to the trouble and come herself to request annulment (Ri ben Malkitzedek, Nedarim 8b). Others explain that perhaps because of his trouble he will add to his wife's words of regret so that they will release her oath or vow (Tosafot and Rosh, ibid.).

and he does not become an agent to release a ban for his wife. Because of the severity of the ban, one who was banned in his presence must be present himself at the time of release of the ban (Hilchot Talmud Torah 7:13, Lechem Mishneh; and see She'iltot of Rav Achai Gaon, Miketz 29). Some read here 'and he does not become an agent to release a vow for his wife,' and explain that only when the wife has already regretted may the husband come and request annulment from the court, but if she has not yet regretted and the judges must find an opening to cause her to regret, she must come herself to court (Shiurei Rabbi Yosef Dov Soloveitchik, Nedarim 8b; and see Ra'avad and Lechem Mishneh, who explained this reading differently). Some explained, according to this reading, that the husband himself cannot join the releasers (Radbaz, and see Piskei VeShitot).
for only the husband or the father can annul. For they can annul the vow even against the wife's will and even without regret and the like (see Hilchot Nedarim 13:2).
and they release at night. Although they do not do so when it is a matter of law (Hilchot Sanhedrin 3:3, 3:7).
therefore. Since the release of oaths and vows is not considered a legal proceeding, for one does not judge on the Sabbath (Hilchot Shabbat 23:14).

if it was for the needs of the Sabbath. Unlike annulment by a father or husband, who may annul on the Sabbath even oaths and vows not needed for the Sabbath, because they can annul only on the same day they heard (Hilchot Shabbat 24:6, Hilchot Nedarim 13:8).
and he answered amen or accepted the oath. As explained above 2:1.
they release him only in the presence of Reuben who administered the oath. So that he not suspect him of having violated his oath without annulment.
swore on the knowledge of the many. He made his oath depend on the knowledge of the many (see also above 2:15).
they never release him. For release is effective only for a vow that depends on the knowledge of the one who vows himself, and not for a vow that depends on the knowledge of many.
that he will never benefit from so-and-so. That he will not receive benefit from so-and-so or from several people living in the city, such as receiving payment.
and the people of that city needed. And among them the man or men from whom he swore not to benefit.
to teach Torah. In the ways in which a teacher is permitted to receive payment for teaching Torah to others (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 1:7, Hilchot Nedarim 6:7).
to slaughter. To slaughter.
and only this one was found. The one who swore is the only one who knows these crafts, and he needs to release his vow so that he can receive payment from them for his work.
and came to court to fulfill his oath. For example, he swore to divorce his wife, as below, or he came to court to consult about what to do.
that he will regret. That he will repent.
and stood in his rebelliousness. He remained in his opposition.
a bad name. An evil reputation.

and you cannot take her back. Like a divorced woman who married another, who is forbidden to her first husband and he can no longer marry her even if she is divorced from the second (Hilchot Gerushin 11:12).

one does not open with something newly arisen. Even when the judges find an opening for the one who swore in order to release his vow (as above halakhah 10), they do not open with something that did not exist when he vowed and arose afterward.
the town scribe. The one who writes documents for the townspeople.
since he has not yet regretted, only wants that he not benefit from him and that he not become a scribe. So the new development did not cause him to regret his vow, and he still wants it.
but if he himself regretted because of the new development and his mind turned, they release him. Because the new development caused him to regret his vow, as above halakhah 1.
he asks about the last oath first. For if he asks about the first, he violates his second oath.
and he is a nazirite if he asks about this oath. He swore that he would be a nazirite if he asks about his first oath.

and he asked about the first oath and it was released, he is liable for the second oath. For the second oath did not take effect because of the first, and when he asked about the first, the second oath found room to take effect.

he asked about the third only, he is liable for the first and second. Although one cannot release an oath that has not yet taken effect (as above halakhah 14), this applies to an oath dependent on time or condition. But in this case, where the oaths are fit to take effect at the same time and do not take effect only because an oath does not take effect on an oath, he may release whichever he wishes, and the others will take effect (Ben Yedid, Me'irat Einayim).
as we have explained. Above 4:10.
they tied him to be flogged. They bound him to the post on which lashes are given.
one who claims money from his friend. For example, he said to him, 'Give me the deposit I have with you.'
that if he admitted it, he would be obligated to pay. Unlike a fine, as below halakhah 2.
and denied and swore. He denied that he has his friend's money and swore to it, for example he said, 'I swear you have nothing with me.'
or the claimant administered the oath to him. He had him swear to return his money.
he is liable for the oath of deposit. He must pay principal and a fifth and bring a guilt offering (as above 1:9).

for in the oath of deposit, one who swears of his own accord is the same etc.. This is unlike an ordinary oath, for which he is not liable without answering amen (as above 2:1), and unlike the oath of testimony, for which he is liable only if he swore in court (as below 9:1).

for his denial after the claimant administered the oath is like answering amen. But if he denied before the claimant administered the oath, and did not answer amen to his oath, this is not like an oath.
for example, he claimed from him a fine. For example, he claimed that he stole his ox and slaughtered or sold it, for which he is liable for the fine of fourfold and fivefold payment (as below 8:1).
for a person does not pay a fine on his own word. Hilchot Genevah 1:5.
he is exempt from the oath of deposit. For the oath of deposit applies only when the oath causes the claimant to lose money.
and he is liable for an oath of utterance. For he swore falsely.
a deposit. Money he placed in his hand.
and they remain before their owners and in their possession. For land is not robbed, and it always remains in the possession of its owners (see Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 9:1).

slaves who were equated with land. They were made equivalent to them in halakhah, as learned from the verse 'you shall hold them as a possession for your children' (Leviticus 25:46, Hilchot Genevah 2:2).
for their bodies are not money. They are not actual money but evidence of ownership of money.
to his agent who comes with his authorization. The agent has in his hand a letter of authorization from the litigant stating that he permits him to litigate his matter and collect money.
in a language he knows. In a language he understands.
even though he swore falsely and witnesses warned him at the time of his oath. And one who swears a false oath deliberately receives lashes (as above 1:3).
as we have explained. Above 1:9.

for had he admitted after denying, he would be obligated to pay, even though he denied in court. His denial does not exempt him from paying, unlike the oath of testimony, where if they denied and afterward admitted they do not testify, and therefore if they denied four or five times they are liable only once (as below 10:18).
he is liable for only one sacrifice. Since there is only one oath here.
he is liable for each one. For he specified an oath for each one.
he is liable only once. Since he swore one oath about all these kinds of money.

and even if he had in his hand one perutah from all of them. Although one who is claimed for less than the value of a perutah is exempt from the oath of deposit (as below halakhah 16), here, where he swore one oath on several things, they combine to the value of a perutah, and he is liable.
and it turns out this one is liable for twenty guilt offerings. For he swore a separate oath to five people, and each one claims from him four kinds of money.
he pays the first principal. But he does not pay principal more than once.
and one fifth for each and every oath. Besides the guilt offering he must bring for each and every oath.
he pays seven. Four perutot of principal, plus three perutot which are three fifths, a fifth for each oath.
less than a perutah is not money. In halachic terms (see for example Hilchot Gezelah 1:6).
and he is liable for a vain oath. For he swore falsely.

and slaughtered it or sold it. He slaughtered it or sold it to another; the law is that he pays a fine of five times the value of the ox, and if he stole a sheep he pays four times its value ("the fourfold and fivefold payments," Hilchot Genevah 1:6).
as will be explained in Hilchot Genevah. 1:5.
exempt from the oath of deposit. For one is liable for it only if he denied something that would obligate him to pay money.
Your ox killed my slave. And the owner of the ox must pay a fine of thirty shekels to the master (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 11:1).
You knocked out my tooth and blinded my eye. The law is that the slave goes free from his master, and this is considered a fine to the master (Hilchot Avadim 5:17).
but he is liable for a vain oath. For he swore falsely.
as we have explained. Above 7:2.
in a matter involving both a fine ... and money. That the claim includes both a fine and money.

You raped or seduced my daughter. The rapist must pay a fine of fifty shekels, and in addition payments for shame, blemish and pain according to assessment. The seducer is subject to the same law, except that he does not pay for pain (Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 2:1-3).

had he admitted, he would pay for shame and blemish on his own admission. And likewise pain in the case of the rapist (see Kesef Mishneh, Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 2:12); thus this is an oath involving a monetary obligation.
You stole my ox. A thief must pay twice the value of the theft: the first payment is the principal, and the second payment ("double") is a fine (Hilchot Genevah 1:4).
You wounded me. One who wounds another must pay him five things: damage, pain, healing, loss of time, and shame. These are not a fine but money (Hilchot Chovel 1:1).

Your ox killed my ox. This refers to a forewarned ox that killed another ox, whose owner must pay full damages to the owner, and this has the law of money. But if an ordinary (tam) ox killed another ox, he pays its owner only half damages as a fine, and if he swore he is not liable for it (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 2:7-8).
and it was stolen or lost. An unpaid custodian is exempt for theft and loss.
for had he admitted and said the matter as it was. That he would admit that the ox died.
because he is an unpaid custodian. And an unpaid custodian is exempt if the animal died (Hilchot Sechirut 1:2).
for he did not exempt himself from payment by his denial. A borrower is liable for theft and loss, so he did not exempt himself from paying money.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot She'elah U'Pikadon 1:1.
in any case. In every case.
for if the ox was stolen or lost after this admission, he would be exempt from paying. By the law of an unpaid custodian; thus he exempted himself from payment in these cases.
that he rented it. A renter is liable for theft and loss, but exempt if it broke or died; thus he saved himself from payment in these cases.
as will be explained in Hilchot She'elah. That a borrower is exempt when the animal died as a result of work (Hilchot She'elah U'Pikadon 1:1); thus he exempted himself from payment in this case.
for he admitted the principal and did not exempt himself at all by this denial. Since he returns the ox, his oath does not exempt him from payment in any way.
for he denied money. Even if he admitted to the other partner, he has exempted himself from paying the first partner's share.
and admitted everything to one of them. He admitted that he owes the entire amount, but not to the partners, only to one of them.
a loan by document. That the lender holds a document as proof of the loan.
for by the document the land is mortgaged. And the lender can collect his debt from the land, even if the borrower sold it to others.
and we have already explained. Above 7:3.
in its time. At its proper time.

that the defendant becomes liable by their testimony alone. But if he could be made to pay even without their testimony, for example if there is another pair of witnesses, they are exempt (as below 10:15).
and denied their testimony and swore. They denied knowing testimony for him, and swore to that effect.
whether they swore outside the court. Provided that they deny it in the court (as below, halachah 2).
are liable for the oath of testimony. And they must bring an olah ve'yored (variable) offering (as above 1:12).
if the claimant adjured them and they denied it. That he adjured them to testify for him, and they said they know no testimony for him.

provided that he adjured them in court. Since in this case the oath is accepted through the denial, without answering amen, it must be clear that the denial refers to the oath; and since the denial must be in court, the oath too must be in court (Noda BiYehudah Kama, Yoreh Deah 66).
or adjured them outside the court. Only if they answered amen after his oath; but if they did not answer amen and only denied, the oath too must be in court, as above.
a place where he would tell and it would help. For only if he testifies in court does his testimony help to obligate the defendant to pay, and his testimony is of no help outside court.
testimony that does not obligate money. As detailed below in chapter 10.

which Scripture specified in the passage. In the passage dealing with the oath of deposit (Leviticus 5:21), as explained above 7:4; and the Sages equated the oath of testimony to the oath of deposit by a gezerah shavah (Shevuot 33b, 35a).
and when they testify, this one will pay. That in these cases their testimony will obligate the defendant to give money or movable property to the claimant.
one who adjures witnesses of a fine. That he adjures them to give testimony that would obligate the defendant to pay him a fine (see also above 8:1-2).

because if the defendant anticipated and admitted the fine, he would be exempt from paying. For one who admits to an act that obligates him to pay a fine is exempt from paying the fine (Hilchot Genevah 1:5).
the witnesses are found not to obligate him by their testimony alone. Thus the defendant's liability does not stem from their testimony alone.

and similarly if the defendant adjured them ... and they denied, they are exempt from the oath of testimony. As it says: "If he does not tell, he shall bear his iniquity" (Leviticus 5:1), and it was handed down to the Sages that the word "lo" is written with both a vav and an alef so that we read it "if he does not tell it to him (lo), he shall bear his iniquity" - specifically to the claimant; but if he does not tell someone else who is not the claimant or the claimant's agent, he is not liable (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 4:12).
and he heard the voice of adjuration and he is a witness. That he heard the voice of an oath ("alah") when he had already witnessed the event.
who knows testimony for me. This refers to one who knows now (that is how the future form "yeda" is interpreted), for knowledge of the testimony must precede the oath (as above, halachah 7).

because he did not single out his witnesses for an oath by themselves. Because he did not explicitly adjure all those standing there but meant to adjure only whoever knows testimony for him, and since the claimant does not know who knows and who does not, he did not single out his witnesses (Torat Chayim, Shevuot 35a).
and they denied it. And they themselves did not swear, and he did not adjure them a second time.

I adjure all those standing here that if they know testimony for me, they shall come and testify for me, etc.. Since he explicitly adjured everyone standing there, his witnesses are included among them, and this oath counts as singling out the witnesses (Torat Chayim ibid., Ran, Shevuot 15b).

and his witnesses were among them. And they answered amen together with everyone, and after some time he demanded that they testify for him and they denied it in court. Or this gathering took place in a synagogue where there was a court (as below).
for he had first demanded it of them. Therefore, even though he adjured them in wording that does not constitute singling out, the demand he first made of them constitutes singling out.
and there is a court there. Then they are liable even if they did not answer amen, as explained above, halachah 1.
as we have explained. Above 2:2.
that the claimant demands it of them. Or his agent (see above, halachot 6-7).
but he is liable for a vain oath. And he is liable to lashes if he did it intentionally, and if inadvertently he brings an olah ve'yored offering (above 1:3).
provided that he swore or answered amen if another adjured him. As above 2:1.
he is not liable for a vain oath, but only for the oath of testimony. Therefore he does not receive lashes, but only brings an offering.

for Scripture excluded the oath of testimony from the category of vain oath, to obligate one who does it intentionally, like one who does it inadvertently, to bring an offering and not lashes. Although the oath of testimony is a kind of vain oath, Scripture removed it from the category of vain oath, and obligates the intentional offender in the same way as the inadvertent one (unlike a vain oath, where the inadvertent offender brings an offering and the intentional offender receives lashes, above 1:3).

as it says: "of one of these," etc.. From here we learn that he cannot be given an additional liability for having intentionally violated a vain oath, since Scripture says: "Or if a person swears, speaking rashly with his lips ... and it is hidden from him, and he knew, and he is guilty of one of these," and the Sages expounded that one cannot be liable for several kinds of oaths together, only for one kind of oath (Shevuot 25b; see also above 7:8).
in the way we explained regarding the oath of deposit. Above 7:11-14.
in a matter that has both a negative and a positive. That one may swear about it both to do and not to do, as learned from the verse: "to do evil or to do good" (Leviticus 5:4).
and since this negative aspect of it is not a vain oath. For the negative side of this oath is the oath of testimony.
disqualified. A person who committed a transgression for which the Torah mandates lashes is called wicked and is disqualified from testifying (Hilchot Edut 10:2).
or a relative. Who is disqualified from testifying by Torah law (ibid. 13:1).
even if disqualified from testifying by rabbinic law. For example, a person who committed a transgression forbidden by the Sages and is disqualified from testifying rabbinically (ibid. 10:3).
or if the king was one of his witnesses, who is unfit to testify. For the Sages decreed that the kings of Israel may not testify (Hilchot Melachim 3:7).
or if they were hearsay witnesses. And one who heard from another witness is disqualified from testifying (Hilchot Edut 17:1).
for had they admitted. That they know testimony for the claimant, and would testify.
the defendant would not become liable for money by saying it. For he does not become obligated by this statement to give money to his fellow (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 4:8).

that he is not the son of a divorcee. For the son of a divorcee is disqualified from the priesthood by Torah law (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 19:3), and he wants them to testify in order to qualify him for the priesthood.
or the son of a chalutzah. Who is disqualified from the priesthood by rabbinic law (ibid., halachah 8).
that his son wounded him. And one who strikes his father and makes a wound is liable to the death penalty by a court (Hilchot Chovel 4:7).
and that so-and-so set his stack on fire on Shabbat. And he incurred stoning for kindling on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 7:1).
and that so-and-so raped or seduced his betrothed daughter. And one who has relations with a betrothed girl is liable to stoning (Hilchot Sanhedrin 15:10).

and he is not liable to pay, as we explained in Hilchot Na'arah. 1:10; that when a person committed an act for which, if done intentionally, he is liable to the death penalty by a court, he is not liable to payments for it (and see also Hilchot Chovel there).
for the testimony of one witness does not obligate money. Hilchot Edut 5:1.

for had they testified, they would cause her to lose her ketubah, and this claimant would be exempt. For a husband whose wife committed adultery is exempt from paying her ketubah (Hilchot Ishut 24:6).
witnesses of warning. That the husband told his wife in their presence not to be secluded with a certain man.

or witnesses of seclusion. Who saw the woman secluded with that man. Through the witnesses of warning and seclusion she is made to drink the bitter waters of a sotah in order to test her (Hilchot Sotah 1:1-2).

even though this testimony causes her to lose her ketubah if she does not drink. For if she wishes, the woman can say that she became defiled, or say "I am not defiled and I will not drink," and she leaves her husband without a ketubah (ibid. 2:1).
and she does not forfeit her ketubah. And she does not lose her ketubah.

as we explained in Hilchot Sotah. 1:14; that when there are witnesses of warning and seclusion, one witness suffices to testify that she committed adultery in order to forbid her to her husband and cause her to leave without a ketubah.

and he adjured one witness to come and testify for him that this person owes him a maneh. Although a single witness does not obligate money, he does obligate the defendant to take an oath (ibid. 1:1).

for had he testified, this defendant would pay money on his testimony. For when the defendant is suspected regarding oaths, the claimant swears and takes what he claimed, and when both are suspected regarding oaths the oath returns to the defendant, and since he cannot swear, he pays.
as will be explained in Hilchot To'en. 2:4.
for example, where the claimant and the defendant were suspected regarding oaths. For example, that they swore falsely (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 2:1-2).

for had he testified, she could remarry and collect her ketubah. For one witness is believed to testify to a woman that her husband died, and she may remarry on his word (Hilchot Gerushin 12:15), and then she can collect her ketubah from the heirs of her first husband.

where she was entitled to collect her ketubah from movable property. For example, if it was written in the ketubah that she can collect it both from land and from movable property (since by strict law a ketubah is collected only from land, see Hilchot Ishut 16:5-9).
and similarly if there were two. Even if two witnesses know such testimony, since it is a liability of land, they are exempt.
as we explained. Above 9:3.

for example, where the second begins to deny within the time of speaking of his fellow. Within the time it takes to say the words "Shalom aleicha, Rabbi" (above 2:17), in which case the denial is considered a single denial.
his testimony did not obligate money. For after his fellow's denial he became a single witness and has no power to obligate money; thus his denial does not withhold money from the claimant.
relatives of the claimant or of the defendant through their wives. And they are disqualified from testifying for them.
even though these will soon be qualified when the dying women die. For upon the death of these women they will no longer be relatives of the claimant or defendant and will be able to testify.
these are exempt from the oath of testimony as we explained. Above 9:2; that a denial outside the court does not obligate.
where they answered amen. When the claimant adjured them.
these are exempt until he adjures them in court and they deny it there. Then they become liable for the last oath, but not for all the oaths with which he adjured them earlier.
as we explained. Above 9:1.

because after they denied in court, if they went back and admitted, their testimony is not testimony and is of no use at all. For a witness who testified or swore before a court about a particular matter cannot go back and say the opposite (see Mishnah Shevuot 4:3, Hilchot Edut 3:5).
as we explained. Above 9:14.

for swearing by His great and holy Name is one of the ways of service. As the verse begins: "You shall fear the Lord your God, and Him you shall serve, and to Him you shall cling, and by His name you shall swear" (Deuteronomy 6:13, and similarly ibid. 10:20).

and a person is permitted to swear to fulfill a commandment ... even though he is already sworn to it from Mount Sinai. And although he swore by the Name of God, this is not considered taking the Name of Heaven in vain and is not a false oath (for the law of one who swears to fulfill a commandment see above 5:16).
there are three kinds of oaths for which one is liable by Torah law. See also Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:1-2.

one whose fellow claimed movable property from him. He claimed from his fellow that he holds some of his movable property, as a deposit or loan and the like (unlike land, slaves and documents, about which one does not swear by Torah law, see ibid. 5:1).
and one witness testifies against him. For unlike two witnesses, a single witness has no power to extract money, only to obligate an oath.
a definite claim and a denial. A definite claim by the claimant that he is owed, and a denial of the claim by the defendant.
swears out of doubt. He swears on a claim of doubt, unlike the previous cases in which he swears on a definite claim.
the oath of a hired worker. A hired worker who claims against the employer that he did not pay him his wages, and the employer claims he paid (Hilchot Sechirut 11:6).

and one who impugns his document. When the borrower claims he repaid the loan in full, while the lender claims he was repaid only part of the sum, and by this statement he impugns the validity of the document, the lender swears about this (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 14:1).

the oath of partners and sharecroppers. They swear lest they robbed the partner or the owner, or lest they were not careful in the accounting between them, and the like (Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 9:1).

the oath of hesset. When the defendant denies everything, although by Torah law he is not obligated to swear, the Sages imposed an oath on him, since it is reasonable to assume that a person does not make a claim against his fellow for no reason.
and it is an enactment of the Sages of the Talmud. Unlike the other rabbinic oaths (detailed above), which were enacted by the Sages of the Mishnah.
it is not called the oath of the judges. For the difference between it and the oath of the judges see below, halachah 13 (and see also halachot 14-15, 19).
with a curse. A curse (see above 2:2).
and my teachers ruled that the oath of the judges is administered only in the holy tongue. For the opinion of the Rambam himself, see below, halachah 14.
he is cursed to the Lord. And he means it with regard to himself.
holding an object. A term for an oath taken while holding a sacred object (such as a Torah scroll).
for he has taken hold of a Torah in his hand, and they are like a book. For tefillin have passages of the Torah written in them.

a Torah scholar is, from the outset, adjured while seated with tefillin in his hand. Since it is the way of a Torah scholar to honor and glorify tefillin and be careful with their sanctity (Meiri, Rabbi Yitzchak Ze'ev Soloveitchik's lessons, Shevuot 38b).
tefillin in his palm is an object. So the reading in the manuscript; possibly "hi" (it) refers to the tefillin under the influence of Arabic.
as we explained. Above, halachah 8.
that they adjure only in the holy tongue. Because it carries an element of fear and deterrence (Radbaz), or because of the honor of the court (Kesef Mishneh).
and it is not proper to rely on this ruling. Because the one swearing must understand the oath that he utters.
until he is familiar with the language of the oath. That he understands the intent of the words and their meaning.

for the oath of the judges is the oath of deposit itself. For he denies a monetary claim that his fellow has against him (as above 1:8), and just as one is not liable for the oath of deposit unless he is adjured in a language he knows (as above 7:7), so too for the oath of the judges.
does not need intimidation. Because in a claim of doubt it is possible that both are telling the truth, there is no need to intimidate in order to deter from a false oath (Mirkevet HaMishneh).

for the whole world trembled at the time when the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain". For this commandment was stated at Mount Sinai, where the whole world trembled, and this commandment in particular carries special severity, as described here (see Shevuot 39a).
he will clear. Although it says, "He will by no means clear," our Sages expounded: "'He will clear' - for those who repent; 'He will not clear' - for those who do not repent" (Shevuot 39a).

will not clear. For regarding a false oath it says: "For the Lord will not clear one who takes His name in vain," and since it does not say "he will clear" about it, this implies that even if he repents it does not help him without further repayment (as below 12:1).
who protect him. Who shield him.
the enemies of Israel. This means the people of Israel, but it is a euphemism.
guarantors. Responsible.
swearing and denying. A false oath and denial.

they suspend it for him for two or three generations if he has merit. When he has merits from fulfilling the Torah and its commandments, they wait to punish him for several generations, and only afterward, if his children continue in his sins, they collect from them (see Mechilta DeRashbi 20:5, Berakhot 7a).

I have brought it forth. And the previous verse says: "And he said to me, This is the curse that goes out over the face of the whole land, for every one who steals shall be cleared out according to it, and every one who swears shall be cleared out according to it," so it is a curse that will come on a thief who swears falsely.
they exempt him. From the obligation of the oath.

these wicked men. Even where the claimant is telling the truth he is called wicked, because he was not careful to deposit his money with a trustworthy person or to do so before witnesses, and caused the Name of Heaven to be taken in vain. And where the defendant is telling the truth he is called wicked because he should have been careful in his actions and prevented the possibility of a claim against him (see Radbaz). It can also be explained to mean that surely one of them is lying, either the claimant or the defendant (Rabbeinu Chananel, Shevuot 47b).

we do not adjure you according to your own mind but according to our mind and the mind of the court. When the oath is according to their mind, his oath is subject to the mind and intention of the judges, and he cannot make a condition in his heart or intend his oath for some other matter (as above 2:16).
as we explained. Above, halachah 15.

and not by the oath of hesset. Although the oath of hesset involves a definite claim by the claimant, since it does not involve holding an object (as above, halachah 13), it is less severe than the other oaths on a definite claim, and therefore one does not intimidate with it.
to urge. To plead with them not to swear.
for its laws have already been explained. Above 1:8-11.
if there is a house there. When the Temple exists.
as we explained. Above 1:9.
as we explained in Hilchot Teshuvah. 1:2 (and see ibid. halachah 4, Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 5:10).
and they show them that this is an oath, etc.. They create the impression for them that these oaths are valid oaths, by requiring that an opening be found to release the vow (as above 6:10).
his mind is on the mentions. On the names of God in the Torah, and so his oath is an oath.
and if he swore by it without specification. For example, he said "I swear by the Torah," and did not say "by what is written in the Torah."
his mind is on the parchment. On the parchment on which the Torah scroll is written, and there is no oath here.
he took it in his hand and swore by it. Even if he swore without specification.

if he is a Torah scholar he does not need to ask a sage. Since he knows how to distinguish between one who swears without specification and one who swears by what is written in it, he will not come to treat it lightly and swear even by what is written in it.

his teacher need not compel him, and after he swore he is as before he swore. He need not force him to do the opposite of his oath so that it will not take effect, because it does not take effect in any case (and compare the law of a slave who vowed nazirite status or other vows, Hilchot Nezirut 2:17-18).

minors who swore, etc.. This refers to a boy of twelve years or younger and a girl of eleven years or younger, whose oath at this age is not an oath, and nevertheless they are compelled to keep it so that they will be careful about oaths. But once the boy reaches twelve years and a day, and the girl eleven years and a day, if they swore or vowed and know in whose name they swore or vowed, they are bound to keep their word (see Hilchot Nedarim 11:1-4; Keter HaMelech, Rabbi Yosef Kafih). Some hold that according to the Rambam the law of oaths is not the same as vows on this point, and as long as they have not become adults (a male of thirteen years and a day and a female of twelve years and a day who have produced signs of adulthood, Hilchot Ishut 2:1, 2:10) their oath is not an oath, and nevertheless they are compelled to keep their words so that they do not treat oaths lightly (Knesset HaGedolah, Hagahot Beit Yosef, Yoreh Deah 233).
an unnecessary blessing. One who recites a blessing in a situation where he is not obligated to.
as we explained in Hilchot Berakhot. 1:15.
to excommunicate him. To say to him: "So-and-so is under a ban (shamta)," whereupon he becomes bound by the practices of one under a ban (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 7:2-4).

is nothing but a trace of heresy. Because the release of vows and oaths has no basis in the Written Torah but is learned through the tradition of the Sages from Moses our teacher (as above 6:2), one who is hesitant to do this appears to be denying the tradition of the Oral Torah.

and we are not to attend to releasing except for a matter of a commandment or a great need. Unlike vows, where a person is commanded to have his vow annulled out of concern that he will not keep it (Hilchot Nedarim 13:25), with an oath, which contains the Name of God and whose punishment is great, it is better that he keep his oath than that he release it.

and if he transgressed and swore, he should suffer and keep his oath. If he nevertheless swore and finds it hard to keep the oath, it is better for him to keep his oath and not release it, even though it involves suffering.
swore to do evil and does not change. Even if he swore to harm himself and has distress in keeping the oath, he should not change his word but keep it.
